title: The Emergency Fund — Your Financial Airbag
tagline: How many months you actually need, and exactly where to park it so it beats inflation slightly but stays 100% accessible. Savings account vs liquid fund, settled.
summary: Sizing the emergency fund and choosing where to keep it (savings vs liquid funds vs sweep-in FD).

sections.title: What it is and why it comes before investing

paragraphs: An **emergency fund** is a pot of money set aside only for genuine emergencies: a job loss, a medical bill, an urgent trip home, a phone or laptop you need for work dying. It is *not* for a sale, a trip, or a new gadget — those are planned goals, not emergencies.

It is the **first** financial goal, before any SIP, because it is what keeps your investments invested. Without it, the first shock forces you to either sell investments at a bad time or swipe a credit card at 40% interest. The emergency fund absorbs the shock so your wealth engine keeps running.

blocks.title: The airbag
blocks.text: You hope to never use it, you don't judge it by its 'returns', and you'd never remove it to save weight. An emergency fund is an airbag for your finances: its entire job is to be there, intact, on the one bad day.

sections.title: How many months? The strict rule

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Keep 3 to 6 months of essential expenses (your 'needs', not your full income). 3 months if your income is very stable (secure salaried job, family support). 6 months — or more — if your income is variable, you're a sole earner, or your job is insecure.

paragraphs: Note the base is **monthly needs, not income**. In an emergency you cut wants instantly, so you only need to cover essentials. For Aarav, needs are about **₹15,000/month** (rent, food, transport, phone, misc).

blocks.title: Aarav's target
blocks.expression: Target  =  Monthly needs  ×  Months of cover

blocks.text: ₹60,000 from a ₹3,000/month savings habit takes ~20 months. That's fine — build it in stages. A first milestone of even ₹15,000 (one month) already prevents most small crises from becoming credit-card debt. Build the fund *before* starting long-term equity SIPs.

sections.title: Where to park it: the real question

paragraphs: Two rules govern *where* the emergency fund lives: it must be **100% safe** (no chance of losing capital) and **highly liquid** (reachable within minutes to a day). Returns are a distant third priority — but with a small tweak you can still beat a plain savings account and soften inflation.

blocks.title: The realistic parking options (illustrative 2026 rates)
rows: Keep ~1 month here for instant access
Great hybrid — savings access, FD-ish rate
Best home for the bulk of the fund
NEVER — not safe, defeats the purpose
blocks.caption: Returns are illustrative and change with rates. The ranking on safety and liquidity is what matters.

blocks.title: The recommended split for Aarav
blocks.text: Keep ~₹15,000 (one month) in his savings account for instant access, and the remaining ~₹45,000 in a liquid fund or sweep-in FD earning ~6–7%. He gets instant money for small shocks, a slightly inflation-beating return on the bulk, and zero risk to capital.

blocks.title: Why not just chase higher returns?
blocks.text: An emergency fund in equity or a long lock-in FD fails exactly when you need it: markets can be down 30% on the day you lose your job, and a locked FD charges a penalty to break early. Liquidity and safety beat yield here, every time.

blocks.title: On liquid funds and inflation
blocks.text: A liquid fund's ~6–7% won't make you rich and roughly tracks or slightly trails inflation after tax — that's the point. The emergency fund's job is preservation and access, not growth. Your *long-term* money does the growing (Modules 2, 4, 5).

cheatsheet: Emergency fund = 3–6 months of essential expenses (needs, not full income); 6+ if income is unstable.
Two non-negotiables: 100% safe and highly liquid. Returns come a distant third.
Split: ~1 month in savings (instant), the rest in a liquid fund / sweep-in FD at ~6–7%.
Never park the emergency fund in equity or a locked FD — it fails right when you need it.
Build the emergency fund before starting long-term equity SIPs.

questions.prompt: Aarav's monthly take-home is ₹20,000 but his essential expenses are ₹15,000. Should his 4-month emergency fund be ₹80,000 or ₹60,000?
questions.hint: What does the fund actually need to cover during an emergency?
answer: ₹60,000. The fund is sized on **essential expenses (₹15,000), not income (₹20,000)**. In a real emergency you immediately cut wants and discretionary spending, so you only need to cover needs. ₹15,000 × 4 = ₹60,000. Sizing it on full income would over-park safe money that could otherwise be growing in long-term investments.
keyPoints: Base on essential expenses, not income
Wants get cut in an emergency

questions.prompt: A friend suggests Aarav put his entire ₹60,000 emergency fund into an index fund 'so it at least grows 12%'. Why is this a dangerous idea?
questions.hint: When do emergencies and market crashes often coincide?
answer: An emergency fund must be safe and instantly available. Equity index funds can fall 30–50% in a downturn — and downturns often coincide with the very emergencies you'd need the money for (recessions cause layoffs). If Aarav loses his job in a crash, he'd be forced to sell units at a big loss to pay rent.
The right home is a liquid fund or sweep-in FD: ~6–7%, capital-safe, reachable in a day. The fund's job is preservation and access, not growth — growth is what his *separate* long-term SIPs are for.
keyPoints: Equity can be down 30%+ exactly when needed
Preservation + access > yield for this money

questions.prompt: Why split the fund between a savings account and a liquid fund instead of putting it all in one?
questions.hint: Trade-off between instant access and a better return.
answer: It balances the two needs. A savings account gives **instant** access (UPI/debit at 2am) but a poor ~3% return. A liquid fund gives a better ~6–7% but redemptions may take until the next day (though many now offer instant redemption up to ₹50,000).

Keeping about one month in savings covers any sudden, same-minute need, while the bulk sits in the liquid fund earning more and softening inflation. You get the best of both: immediacy for small shocks, better yield on the rest.
keyPoints: One month instant + rest in liquid fund
